title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
Criminals deployed generative AI and deepfake technology to impersonate real people, including a South Florida immigration attorney, to defraud victims. The scammers used voice cloning sourced from social media, spoofed phone numbers, and fake photographs to make their impersonations credible. The deployment required no technical sophistication beyond access to generative AI tools and social media data. What would have caught this: verification by victims through trusted channels and direct contact with the alleged person using known contact information before sending money.

The failure happened in the victims' decision process, not in the AI system itself. The systems that generated the deepfakes and voice clones performed as designed. Victims lost money because they did not verify the identity of people requesting funds through independent channels. No safeguard in the AI systems prevented their use for impersonation, and the scammers faced no technical barrier to deploying them at scale.

It is not established whether the AI vendors knew their systems were being used for fraud, what steps they took to prevent misuse, or whether terms of service prohibited this use.

summary:
Criminals are increasingly using artificial intelligence to create convincing deepfakes and voice clones for scams across Georgia and South Florida. Recent cases include a Cobb County couple losing roughly $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scam and a South Florida immigration attorney discovering his voice and identity were cloned to target immigrants. According to the FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report, Americans reported nearly $893 million in AI-enabled scam losses last year. Florida experienced 350 AI-related complaints totaling nearly $39.9 million in losses, while Georgia had 71 complaints resulting in more than $10.4 million in losses.

Scammers use generative AI to clone voices from social media, spoof phone numbers, create fake photographs, and research personal relationships to make scams appear authentic. Common schemes include the grandparent scam, romance scams, and impersonation attempts. Banks warn customers to verify requests through trusted channels rather than responding immediately. Authorities recommend establishing code words with family members and contacting the person directly through known phone numbers before sending money. Victims should report suspected scams to local law enforcement and the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center.
